details: ISF-2 (Interim Spent Fuel Storage Facility 2): dry cask storage facility at ChNPP site; designed for: all 21,217 RBMK-1000 spent fuel assemblies from Units 1-4; contractor: Holtec International (USA); type: VENTILATED STORAGE MODULES (VSM) system; each cask: 47 assemblies per cask; total casks: ~450; passive air cooling (no active cooling required); design lifetime: 100 years; facility dimensions: ~300m × 160m; regulated by SNRIU; construction 2014-2020; hot operations started 2020 with ISF-1 transfer; expected completion: 2028 (delayed from 2025 due to 2022 occupation)
current_status: ISF-2 vs ISF-1 (wet pool): ISF-1 was 3 wet pools originally holding assemblies from Units 1-3; after Unit 4 accident all Units' fuel required storage; ISF-1 nearing capacity and aging infrastructure; ISF-2 = preferred long-term solution; passive safety: no pumps required → eliminates Fukushima-class station blackout risk; SAFETY ARGUMENT for dry casks: spent fuel after 5+ years cooling: decay heat low enough (<1 kW/assembly) for passive air cooling; thermal design: VSM air flow path removes decay heat by natural convection; temperature in cask: <65°C steady state
source: chernobyl_decommissioning_physics_REAL.csv; IAEA PRIS; SSE CHNPP; Holtec International

details: ISF-2 loading progress: facility started hot operations late 2020; 1,698 assemblies loaded as of January 2022 (before Russian occupation); occupation March-April 2022: loading HALTED; ISF-1 to ISF-2 transfer crane operations suspended due to safety concerns under military occupation; post-occupation (April 2022 onwards): loading resumed at reduced pace; estimated 2026 status: ~4,000-6,000 assemblies transferred (5-10yr process still ongoing); ISF-1 wet pool situation: continues to hold majority of assemblies; ISF-1 pool cooling = active (requires electrical power + pumps); ISF-1 = vulnerability if power lost (unlike passive ISF-2)
current_status: ISF-1 remains Achilles heel: requires active cooling; assemblies in ISF-1 wet pool have been cooling since 1986-2000 (some > 25 years cooled); at 25+ years: decay heat negligible → could be moved to dry cask storage safely; however fuel integrity inspection + documentation required before each assembly transfer; 2022 occupation disrupted: assembly documentation access; SNRIU oversight; international inspection; IAEA increased monitoring of ISF-2 and ISF-1 after occupation; NEA 2024 report details ISF situation under wartime conditions

details: RBMK-1000 spent fuel assembly composition (per assembly; 4-year irradiation at ~15,000 MWd/tHM): initial U: 14.3 kg/assembly (185 kg divided by 13 = ~14.2 kg per bundle group; assembly has 2 fuel bundles of ~92.5 kg each); U-235 remaining: 13.2 kg (initial 14.3 kg × 2.8% enrichment = 0.4 kg → depleted to ~0.6-1.0% = ~0.15 kg per assembly remaining); Pu-239 generated: ~0.22 kg/assembly (0.6 g/MWd × 370 MWd per assembly); Pu-240: ~0.05 kg; Cs-137 in assembly at discharge: ~0.012 kg (Cs-137 per assembly = 260 PBq × 185 kg/ton fuel × ton/1000kg ÷ 1661 channels ÷ 3.19 TBq/g)
current_status: ISF-2 total inventory: 21,217 assemblies × 0.22 kg Pu-239 = 4,668 kg Pu-239 total in storage (significant nuclear material); Cs-137 total: 21,217 assemblies × 0.012 kg Cs-137 × 3.19 TBq/g = 812 TBq Cs-137 in ISF-2 when full; this is 10× Chernobyl's environmental release (85 PBq) = significance of secure dry storage; decay heat per assembly: immediately post-discharge = ~10 kW; after 25 years: ~0.2 kW; passive cooling requirement: 0.2 kW per assembly at 25yr cooling; VSM designed for max 0.8 kW/assembly (fresh 5yr cooled)

details: Spent fuel decay heat: ANS-5.1 (1979/2005) standard; P(t)/P₀ = 0.066 × [t^(-0.2) - (t+t_s)^(-0.2)] where t = cooling time (s); t_s = irradiation time (s); P₀ = reactor operating power; at shutdown (t=0): P(0) = 7% P₀; at t=1 day: P = ~0.5% P₀; at t=1 year: P = ~0.03% P₀; at t=25 years: P = ~0.002% P₀; for single RBMK assembly operating at 3200 MWth ÷ 1661 channels = 1.93 MW per channel: P(0) per assembly = 7% × 1.93 MW = 135 kW; P(25yr) = 0.002% × 1.93 MW = 39 W = 0.039 kW
current_status: Passive safety argument for dry cask storage: 0.039 kW per assembly at 25yr cooling → passive air convection easily removes this heat; comparison: Fukushima BWR assemblies (shorter cooling time; higher power density): even these were demonstrated to not overheat with proper pool level; RBMK assemblies in ISF-2 (all >25yr cooled by 2026): decay heat negligible; air temperature in VSM cask: calculated ΔT < 30°C above ambient for 0.2 kW load; thermal margin: factor 4× safety margin; ISF-2 passive safety = best long-term solution for Chernobyl fuel vs wet storage requiring pumps

details: ISF-2 criticality safety: RBMK spent fuel k_eff must remain <0.95 in VSM casks; criticality control mechanisms: (1) burnup credit: used fuel has less U-235 remaining (depleted from 2.8% to ~0.6-1.0%) → lower fissile loading; (2) geometry: fuel assembly spacing maintained by basket structure; (3) neutron absorption: Gd-containing poison rods in some fuel assemblies; (4) boron carbide shielding in VSM structure; (5) absence of moderator: dry storage → no water moderator → k_eff << 0.95 even without burnable poison; subcritical by design: k_eff estimated <0.8 for full basket with burnup credit; k_eff <0.5 for worst case dry cask without moderation
current_status: RBMK spent fuel criticality: RBMK uses light water coolant during operation but graphite moderator; in dry storage: no moderator (no graphite; no water) → k_eff << 1; Pu-239 concern: 4,668 kg Pu-239 in full ISF-2 = significant fissile inventory; but Pu-239 in spent fuel matrix = embedded in UO2 ceramic pellets; Pu-239 cannot be extracted without reprocessing; criticality safety analysis: credible accident scenario = cask dropped (assembly deformation); seismic event; analyzed in Holtec VSM Safety Analysis Report (SAR); SAR conclusion: k_eff <0.95 for all analyzed configurations including assembly damage scenarios
source: IAEA Safety Series SSG-15; Holtec VSM SAR; chernobyl_decommissioning_physics_REAL.csv

details: ISF-2 radiation dose rates: on contact with loaded VSM module: <2 mSv/hr (Holtec design limit); at 1m from cask: ~0.01-0.05 mSv/hr; at facility perimeter (300m): <1 µSv/hr; dominant radiation: high-energy gamma from Cs-137 (662 keV) in spent fuel; neutron component: significant in ISF-2 (spontaneous fission from Pu-240 and Cm-244 in spent fuel); VSM shielding: outer concrete jacket + steel inner shell; total attenuation: >10,000× at 1m; dose to facility workers: <0.5 mSv/yr (well below 20 mSv/yr limit); radiation monitoring: continuous gamma and neutron sensors at perimeter; IAEA remote monitoring system
current_status: Comparison to ISF-1 wet pool: wet pool has 3m water cover as primary shielding; contact dose at pool edge: similar to ISF-2 surface; advantage of water: efficient neutron moderator + shield; advantage of dry VSM: no water = no Cs-137 dissolved in pool water = no liquid waste; ISF-1 pool water requires continuous ion exchange treatment to remove dissolved fission products; ISF-2 generates NO radioactive liquid waste (sealed casks); significant operational advantage for long-term management; IAEA SALTO reviews have validated ISF-2 design and operations
source: IAEA SSG-15; Holtec VSM design; radiation_shielding_engineering_REAL.csv; chernobyl_decommissioning_physics_REAL.csv

details: Chernobyl Unit 4 corium (Fuel Containing Material = FCM): total ~170-220 tonnes in Rooms 305/2; 217/2; 210/18; 'Elephant's Foot' (Room 217); composition: UO₂ fuel (~23 kg U-235; ~180 kg U-238 per tonne corium); SiO₂ from melted concrete (sand); Fe₂O₃ from structural steel; various fission products (low fraction now due to decay); Pu-239 (~0.6 kg/tonne corium = ~100-130 kg total); Cs-137 fraction: most Cs volatilized during 1986 melt; some retained (a few TBq total); physical form: glassy lava-like (uranium silicate glass); Elephant's Foot: porous ceramic-glass matrix; 'stalactites' hanging from overhead structures
current_status: Current (2026) corium status: Room 305/2 neutron flux stable since 2022 (after doubling 2016-2021 as water percolated through) following NSC drainage improvements; dose at Elephant's Foot: 0.034 mSv/hr (2026) vs 10,000 R/hr in 1986 = 3×10⁸ reduction from decay; corium presents no criticality risk (k_eff << 1 due to geometry and lack of moderator); BUT: corium in contact with water → U/Pu dissolution concern; NSC prevents rain ingress → protecting corium from water contact; corium removal: no viable technology exists (2026); decommissioning plan says: stabilize in NSC for 100 years then assess options; see also corium_fcm_physics_REAL.csv

details: ISF-2 IAEA safeguards: Ukraine is Non-Nuclear Weapons State (NNWS) under NPT; all nuclear material subject to IAEA safeguards; safeguards approach for ISF-2: inventory verification by fuel assembly count and identification; destructive assay of selected assemblies for isotopic verification; containment/surveillance (C/S): cameras at cask loading station; seals on loaded casks; remote data transmission to IAEA Vienna; frequency: annual inspection minimum; monthly remote data review; continuity of knowledge maintained since 2020 loading start; 2022 occupation: IAEA access to ChNPP maintained (unlike ZNPP where safeguards continuity was disrupted)
current_status: ISF-2 safeguards significance: 21,217 RBMK assemblies = significant nuclear material; Pu-239 content of full ISF-2 (~4,668 kg) is non-weapons-grade (high Pu-240 burnup) BUT still subject to IAEA accountancy; Ukraine's transparency: cooperated fully with IAEA safeguards since independence 1991; Budapest Memorandum compliance; contrast with ZNPP situation: Russian occupation = safeguards continuity challenge; ISF-2 IAEA monitoring = model for how peaceful nuclear programs are verified; any diversion of even 1 assembly would be detected within annual inspection cycle
source: IAEA safeguards documentation; ukraine_nuclear_fleet_REAL.csv; zaporizhzhia_npp_2022_2025_REAL.csv; chernobyl_nuclear_terrorism_risk_REAL.csv
